claim: Drosophila appetitive taste responses towards fatty acids are mediated by sweet sensing Gustatory Receptor Neurons (GRNs).
source: Behavioral studies have established that Drosophila appetitive taste responses towards fatty acids are mediated by sweet sensing Gustatory Receptor Neurons (GRNs).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to behavioral studies (Masek and Keene, 2013) and confirmed by experimental data in the manuscript showing that inactivation of sweet GRNs abolishes PER responses to fatty acids.

claim: Sweet GRN activation by fatty acids requires the function of IR25a, IR76b and IR56d genes.
source: Here we show that sweet GRN activation requires the function of the Ionotropic Receptor genes IR25a, IR76b and IR56d.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of fatty acid responses in mutants and rescue experiments presented in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: IR25a and IR76b are expressed in several neurons per sensillum.
source: The former two IR genes are expressed in several neurons per sensillum, while IR56d expression is restricted to sweet GRNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2, demonstrating expression patterns of IR25a and IR76b in multiple GRNs.

claim: IR56d expression is restricted to sweet GRNs.
source: The former two IR genes are expressed in several neurons per sensillum, while IR56d expression is restricted to sweet GRNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5E and F showing complete overlap between IR56d and Gr64f (sweet GRN marker) and no expression in bitter GRNs.

claim: Loss of appetitive behavioral responses to fatty acids in IR25a and IR76b mutant flies can be completely rescued by expression of respective transgenes in sweet GRNs.
source: Importantly, loss of appetitive behavioral responses to fatty acids in IR25a and IR76b mutant flies can be completely rescued by expression of respective transgenes in sweet GRNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C and D, where expression of UAS-IR25a or UAS-IR76b in sweet GRNs restores PER responses to fatty acids.

claim: Appetitive behavioral responses of wild type flies to hexanoic acid reach a plateau at ~1%, but decrease with higher concentration.
source: Interestingly, appetitive behavioral responses of wild type flies to hexanoic acid reach a plateau at ~1%, but decrease with higher concentration, a property mediated through IR25a/IR76b independent activation of bitter GRNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data in Figure 7B showing maximal PER responses at 1% hexanoic acid with reduced responses at 2.5%.

claim: The decrease in PER responses to hexanoic acid at higher concentrations is mediated through IR25a/IR76b independent activation of bitter GRNs.
source: Interestingly, appetitive behavioral responses of wild type flies to hexanoic acid reach a plateau at ~1%, but decrease with higher concentration, a property mediated through IR25a/IR76b independent activation of bitter GRNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6C and D showing that bitter GRN responses to hexanoic acid do not require IR25a or IR76b, and Figure 7C showing that inactivation of bitter GRNs prevents the decrease in PER at high hexanoic acid concentrations.

claim: IR-based receptors mediate different taste qualities through cell-type specific IR subunits.
source: With our previous report on sour taste, our studies suggest that IR-based receptors mediate different taste qualities through cell-type specific IR subunits.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the current data on fatty acid taste and citation to previous work on sour taste (Chen and Amrein, 2017), showing that IR25a and IR76b function in different GRN types with different cell-type specific IR subunits.

claim: Inactivation of sweet GRNs leads to loss of PER responses to both sucrose and fatty acids.
source: Inactivation of sweet GRNs (Gr64f-GAL4/UAS-TNT) leads to loss of PER responses to both sucrose and fatty acids.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, where flies with tetanus toxin-expressing sweet GRNs show abolished PER responses.

claim: Control flies show robust PER responses to fatty acids and sucrose.
source: Control flies (Gr64f-GAL4/+ and UAS-TNT/+) show robust PER responses to fatty acids and sucrose.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A showing PER responses in control genotypes.

claim: Octuple mutant flies lacking all sugar Gr genes exhibit PER responses to fatty acids similar to flies with functional sugar Gr genes.
source: Octuple mutant flies lacking all sugar Gr genes (Gr5aLexA﻿;ΔGr61aΔGr64a-f) exhibit PER responses to fatty acids similar to flies with functional sugar Gr genes (w1118), but they have severely reduced PER response to sucrose.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B comparing PER responses between octuple mutants and wild-type controls.

claim: Octuple mutant flies lacking all sugar Gr genes have severely reduced PER response to sucrose.
source: Octuple mutant flies lacking all sugar Gr genes (Gr5aLexA﻿;ΔGr61aΔGr64a-f) exhibit PER responses to fatty acids similar to flies with functional sugar Gr genes (w1118), but they have severely reduced PER response to sucrose.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B showing significantly reduced sucrose responses in octuple mutants.

claim: The residual PER responses to sucrose of octuple mutant flies is mediated by Gr43a.
source: The residual PER responses to sucrose of octuple mutant flies is mediated by Gr43a (Miyamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Miyamoto et al., 2012.

claim: Sugar Gr genes are dispensable for fatty acid sensing.
source: Sugar Gr genes are dispensable for fatty acid sensing.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1B showing that octuple mutants lacking sugar Gr genes maintain normal fatty acid responses.

claim: Sweet taste neurons of norpA mutant flies have strongly reduced responses to fatty acids, but not sucrose.
source: Moreover, and consistent with this behavioral phenotype, sweet taste neurons of norpA mutant flies had strongly reduced responses to fatty acids, but not sucrose, using a Ca2+ imaging assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutations in norpA affected PER responses to fatty acids, but not to sugars.
source: Use of different taste receptors for mediating the two taste modalities is consistent with the finding that mutations in norpA, which encodes a phospholipase C, affected PER responses to fatty acids, but not to sugars (Masek and Keene, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Masek and Keene, 2013.

claim: NorpA encodes a phospholipase C.
source: Use of different taste receptors for mediating the two taste modalities is consistent with the finding that mutations in norpA, which encodes a phospholipase C, affected PER responses to fatty acids, but not to sugars (Masek and Keene, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the norpA gene, cited from Masek and Keene, 2013.

claim: IR25a and IR76b are enriched in taste neurons.
source: Of particular interest were IR25a and IR76b, because these two genes are enriched in taste neurons (Cameron et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cameron et al., 2010.

claim: IR25a and IR76b are expressed in multiple GRNs per sensillum.
source: We therefore examined the expression of IR-GAL4/QF drivers for both genes and found that they were indeed expressed in multiple GRNs per sensillum (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2 showing expression patterns.

claim: IR25a and IR76b expression largely overlapped in tarsal sensilla.
source: In tarsal sensilla, their expression largely overlapped (Figure 2F) and included the sweet and bitter GRNs that express sugar and bitter Gr genes, respectively (Figure 2B–E), thus identifying them as possible subunits of fatty acid taste receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: IR25a and IR76b are expressed in sweet GRNs that express sugar Gr genes.
source: In tarsal sensilla, their expression largely overlapped (Figure 2F) and included the sweet and bitter GRNs that express sugar and bitter Gr genes, respectively (Figure 2B–E), thus identifying them as possible subunits of fatty acid taste receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B and C showing co-expression with Gr64f.

claim: IR25a and IR76b are expressed in bitter GRNs that express bitter Gr genes.
source: In tarsal sensilla, their expression largely overlapped (Figure 2F) and included the sweet and bitter GRNs that express sugar and bitter Gr genes, respectively (Figure 2B–E), thus identifying them as possible subunits of fatty acid taste receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2D and E showing co-expression with Gr33a.

claim: PER responses were abolished in both IR25a-/- and IR76b-/- flies to hexanoic, octanoic and linoleic acids.
source: To examine a possible role for IR25a and IR76b in fatty acid taste, we conducted PER assays with flies from each mutant strain to hexanoic, octanoic and linoleic acids and found that PER responses were abolished in both IR25a-/- and IR76b-/- flies, a phenotype completely (hexanoic acid and octanoic acid) or partially (linoleic acid) rescued when expression was restored with UAS-IR25a or UAS-IR76b transgenes (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PER assay data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The loss of PER responses to hexanoic and octanoic acids in IR25a and IR76b mutants is completely rescued by transgene expression.
source: To examine a possible role for IR25a and IR76b in fatty acid taste, we conducted PER assays with flies from each mutant strain to hexanoic, octanoic and linoleic acids and found that PER responses were abolished in both IR25a-/- and IR76b-/- flies, a phenotype completely (hexanoic acid and octanoic acid) or partially (linoleic acid) rescued when expression was restored with UAS-IR25a or UAS-IR76b transgenes (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The loss of PER responses to linoleic acid in IR25a and IR76b mutants is partially rescued by transgene expression.
source: To examine a possible role for IR25a and IR76b in fatty acid taste, we conducted PER assays with flies from each mutant strain to hexanoic, octanoic and linoleic acids and found that PER responses were abolished in both IR25a-/- and IR76b-/- flies, a phenotype completely (hexanoic acid and octanoic acid) or partially (linoleic acid) rescued when expression was restored with UAS-IR25a or UAS-IR76b transgenes (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 3A and B showing partial rescue for linoleic acid.

claim: IR25a-/- and IR76b-/- flies showed normal PER responses to sucrose.
source: Additionally, IR25a-/- and IR76b-/- flies showed normal PER responses to sucrose, indicating that the role of these two genes is specific to fatty acid taste and not required for sweet taste to sugars.
evidence: This claim is supported by PER data in Figure 3C and D showing normal sucrose responses in mutants.

claim: The role of IR25a and IR76b is specific to fatty acid taste and not required for sweet taste to sugars.
source: Additionally, IR25a-/- and IR76b-/- flies showed normal PER responses to sucrose, indicating that the role of these two genes is specific to fatty acid taste and not required for sweet taste to sugars.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that mutants have normal sucrose responses but abolished fatty acid responses.

claim: Expression of IR25a in sweet GRNs of IR25a-/- flies restores PER responses to fatty acids to levels indistinguishable from controls.
source: Importantly, when IR25a function was provided in sweet GRNs of IR25a-/- flies, their PER responses were restored to levels indistinguishable from controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of IR76b in sweet GRNs alone rescues PER responses to fatty acids in IR76b-/- flies.
source: Likewise, expression of IR76b in sweet GRNs alone also rescued PER responses to fatty acids in IR76b-/- flies (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 3D.

claim: The functions of IR25a and IR76b are required in sweet GRNs for robust PER responses to fatty acids, but not to sugars.
source: Together, these observations indicate that the functions of IR25a and IR76b are required in sweet GRNs for robust PER responses to fatty acids, but not to sugars.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data showing that expression in sweet GRNs is sufficient for rescue of fatty acid responses but not required for sugar responses.

claim: Sweet GRNs of 5b and 5s sensilla showed robust Ca2+ increases to hexanoic and octanoic acids in wild type flies.
source: In wild type flies, the sweet GRNs of 5b and 5s sensilla showed robust Ca2+ increases to hexanoic and octanoic acids and modest, but significant increases to linoleic acid (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Sweet GRNs of 5b and 5s sensilla showed modest, but significant Ca2+ increases to linoleic acid in wild type flies.
source: In wild type flies, the sweet GRNs of 5b and 5s sensilla showed robust Ca2+ increases to hexanoic and octanoic acids and modest, but significant increases to linoleic acid (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Only weak Ca2+ responses to fatty acids were observed in the 5v-associated sweet GRNs.
source: Only weak Ca2+ responses were observed in the 5v-associated sweet GRNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ca2+ responses to fatty acids were absent in 5b- and 5s-associated sweet GRNs of IR25a-/- or IR76b-/- flies.
source: Importantly, Ca2+ responses were absent in 5b- and 5s-associated sweet GRNs of IR25a-/- or IR76b-/- flies (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 4D and E showing loss of responses in mutants.

claim: Transgene rescue experiments restored Ca2+ increases to fatty acids to the level observed in w1118 control flies.
source: IR25a or IR76b requirement for cellular fatty acid responses was confirmed by transgene rescue experiments, which restored Ca2+ increases to the level observed in w1118 controls flies (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 4D and E.

claim: RNAi knock-down of IR56d led to a significant reduction in PER responses to all fatty acids.
source: RNAi knock-down of one of these genes, IR56d, led to a significant reduction in PER responses to all fatty acids (Figure 5A), while knock-downs of or of mutations in the other six IR genes had no effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by PER assay data in Figure 5A showing reduced responses with IR56d RNAi.

claim: Knock-downs of or mutations in six other candidate IR genes had no effect on PER responses to fatty acids.
source: RNAi knock-down of one of these genes, IR56d, led to a significant reduction in PER responses to all fatty acids (Figure 5A), while knock-downs of or of mutations in the other six IR genes had no effect (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing no effects for other IR genes.

claim: Expression of RNAi against IR56d in sweet GRNs leads to an almost complete loss of GRN activation to hexanoic and octanoic acids.
source: We next expressed GCaMP6m in sweet GRNs, along with the RNAiIR56d construct and carried out Ca2+ imaging experiments of sweet GRNs. As expected, we observed an almost complete loss of GRN activation to hexanoic and octanoic acids (Figure 5B and C), similar as observed for IR25a or IR76b mutants (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 5B and C.

claim: IR56d-GAL4 shows complete overlap with Gr64f in tarsal segments.
source: Finally, we examined expression of an IR56d-GAL4 line in the tarsal segments of the prothoracic leg (Koh et al., 2014). Indeed, antibody staining of tarsi of flies also expressing a marker for sweet GRNs showed complete overlap between IR56d and Gr64f, while no expression was observed in bitter GRNs, labeled by Gr66a-LexA (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5E showing co-localization.

claim: No expression of IR56d was observed in bitter GRNs labeled by Gr66a-LexA.
source: Finally, we examined expression of an IR56d-GAL4 line in the tarsal segments of the prothoracic leg (Koh et al., 2014). Indeed, antibody staining of tarsi of flies also expressing a marker for sweet GRNs showed complete overlap between IR56d and Gr64f, while no expression was observed in bitter GRNs, labeled by Gr66a-LexA (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5F showing no co-localization with Gr66a.

claim: The fatty acid taste receptor in sweet GRNs is composed of at least three subunits: IR25a, IR76b and IR56d.
source: Taken together, these experiments imply that the fatty acid taste receptor in sweet GRNs is composed of at least three subunits, IR25a, IR76b and the more narrowly expressed IR56d subunit.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined genetic and expression data showing that all three genes are required for fatty acid responses in sweet GRNs.

claim: The experiments do not exclude the possibility of a fourth IR being part of a fatty acid taste receptor complex.
source: However, they do not exclude the possibility of yet a fourth IR being part of a fatty acid taste receptor complex.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging limitations of the current data.

claim: Bitter GRNs of both the s- and b-type sensilla strongly responded to denatonium.
source: Bitter GRNs of both the s- and b-type sensilla strongly responded to denatonium, a bitter tasting compound.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 6B showing responses to denatonium.

claim: Strong Ca2+ increases were observed in the 5b-associated bitter GRN to hexanoic acid.
source: Intriguingly, strong Ca2+ increases were also observed in the 5b-associated bitter GRN to hexanoic acid, while octanoic or linoleic acid elicited no significant responses (Figure 6A and B; note that octanoic and linoleic acids could only be tested at 0.2%, due to low solubility; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Octanoic or linoleic acid elicited no significant responses in bitter GRNs.
source: Intriguingly, strong Ca2+ increases were also observed in the 5b-associated bitter GRN to hexanoic acid, while octanoic or linoleic acid elicited no significant responses (Figure 6A and B; note that octanoic and linoleic acids could only be tested at 0.2%, due to low solubility; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 6B showing no significant responses.

claim: Hexanoic acid activates both appetitive and repulsive GRNs.
source: These observations indicate that at least hexanoic acid activates both appetitive and repulsive GRNs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that hexanoic acid activates both sweet GRNs (appetitive) and bitter GRNs (repulsive).

claim: Bitter GRN responses to hexanoic acid did not require IR25a or IR76b.
source: However, and in contrast to sweet GRNs, bitter GRN responses to hexanoic acid did not require IR25a or IR76b (Figure 6C and D), indicating that these neurons employ a different molecular receptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 6C and D showing normal responses in IR25a and IR76b mutants.

claim: Bitter GRNs employ a different molecular receptor than sweet GRNs for hexanoic acid detection.
source: However, and in contrast to sweet GRNs, bitter GRN responses to hexanoic acid did not require IR25a or IR76b (Figure 6C and D), indicating that these neurons employ a different molecular receptor.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that bitter GRN responses to hexanoic acid are IR25a/IR76b-independent while sweet GRN responses are IR25a/IR76b-dependent.

claim: Sweet GRNs reached maximal activation to hexanoic acid at the modest concentration of 1%.
source: Interestingly, sweet GRNs reached maximal activation already at the modest concentration of 1% (Figure 7A, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 7A.

claim: Maximal activation of bitter GRNs to hexanoic acid was reached at the highest applicable concentration (2.5%).
source: In contrast, maximal activation of bitter GRNs was reached at the highest applicable concentration (2.5%; Figure 7A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 7A.

claim: Bitter GRNs might counteract the activity of sweet GRNs above a certain concentration threshold (>1%) and possibly modulate taste behavior.
source: These observations suggest that bitter GRNs might counteract the activity of sweet GRNs above a certain concentration threshold (>1%) and possibly modulate taste behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the dose-response profiles of sweet and bitter GRNs.

claim: w1118 flies exhibited a maximal PER response to hexanoic acid at ~1%, whereas higher concentrations led to a decrease in PER responses.
source: Indeed, w1118 flies exhibited a maximal PER response at ~1%, whereas higher concentrations of hexanoic acid led to a decrease in PER responses (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response PER data in Figure 7B.

claim: When bitter GRNs are inhibited by expressing TNT or Kir2.1, PER responses to hexanoic acid stayed at the same high level or continued to increase with increasing concentration.
source: In contrast, when we inhibited the activity of bitter GRNs by either expressing TNT or the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1, PER responses stayed at the same high level or continued to increase with increasing hexanoic acid concentration (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by PER data in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of bitter GRNs appears to suppress PER responses at high (2.5%) hexanoic acid concentration.
source: Thus, activation of bitter GRNs appears to suppress PER responses at high (2.5%) hexanoic acid concentration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that inhibiting bitter GRNs prevents the decrease in PER at high hexanoic acid concentrations.

claim: Hexanoic acid elicited the same Ca2+ responses in sweet GRNs, regardless of whether functional bitter GRNs were present.
source: To test whether the decrease of sweet GRN responses was mediated through lateral inhibition, we compared Ca2+ responses of sweet GRNs to 2.5% hexanoic acid in the presence and absence of functional bitter GRNs. However, hexanoic acid elicited the same Ca2+ responses in sweet GRNs, regardless of whether functional bitter GRNs were present (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 7D showing no difference in sweet GRN responses with or without functional bitter GRNs.

claim: The decrease of sweet GRN responses to hexanoic acid is not mediated through lateral inhibition from bitter GRNs.
source: To test whether the decrease of sweet GRN responses was mediated through lateral inhibition, we compared Ca2+ responses of sweet GRNs to 2.5% hexanoic acid in the presence and absence of functional bitter GRNs. However, hexanoic acid elicited the same Ca2+ responses in sweet GRNs, regardless of whether functional bitter GRNs were present (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that sweet GRN responses are unchanged when bitter GRNs are inactivated.

claim: IR genes have emerged as a second large gene family encoding chemoreceptors in insects.
source: IR genes have emerged as a second large gene family encoding chemoreceptors in insects.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to Benton et al., 2009 and Croset et al., 2010.

claim: IRs are derived from ionotropic Glutamate Receptors (iGluRs) genes.
source: IRs are derived from ionotropic Glutamate Receptors (iGluRs) genes and expanded in number during arthropod evolution, comprising a family of 61 genes in Drosophila (Benton et al., 2009; Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Benton et al., 2009 and Croset et al., 2010.

claim: The IR gene family comprises 61 genes in Drosophila.
source: IRs are derived from ionotropic Glutamate Receptors (iGluRs) genes and expanded in number during arthropod evolution, comprising a family of 61 genes in Drosophila (Benton et al., 2009; Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Benton et al., 2009 and Croset et al., 2010.

claim: In the Drosophila olfactory system, IRs function as multimeric receptors in coeloconic olfactory sensory neurons (OSN).
source: In the Drosophila olfactory system, IRs function as multimeric receptors in coeloconic olfactory sensory neurons (OSN) and are thought to sense volatile carboxylic acids, amines and aldehydes (Abuin et al., 2011; Benton et al., 2009; Hussain et al., 2016; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: IRs in olfactory neurons are thought to sense volatile carboxylic acids, amines and aldehydes.
source: In the Drosophila olfactory system, IRs function as multimeric receptors in coeloconic olfactory sensory neurons (OSN) and are thought to sense volatile carboxylic acids, amines and aldehydes (Abuin et al., 2011; Benton et al., 2009; Hussain et al., 2016; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Each coeloconic OSN expresses up to four IR genes, including high levels of either IR8a or IR25a.
source: Expression analyses have shown that each coeloconic OSN expresses up to four IR genes, including high levels of either IR8a or IR25a (Abuin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Abuin et al., 2011.

claim: IR25a and IR8a are distinct from other IRs in that they are more conserved to each other and iGluRs.
source: IR25a and IR8a are distinct from other IRs in that they are more conserved to each other and iGluRs, and they share a long amino terminal domain absent in all other IRs (Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Croset et al., 2010.

claim: IR25a and IR8a share a long amino terminal domain absent in all other IRs.
source: IR25a and IR8a are distinct from other IRs in that they are more conserved to each other and iGluRs, and they share a long amino terminal domain absent in all other IRs (Croset et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Croset et al., 2010.

claim: IR based olfactory receptors are tetrameric complexes thought to consist of up to three different subunits that contain at least one core unit (IR8a or IR25a) and two additional IRs that determine ligand binding specificity.
source: These observations, along with functional analyses of basiconic olfactory neurons that express combinations of IR genes, led to a model in which IR based olfactory receptors are tetrameric complexes thought to consist of up to three different subunits that contain at least one core unit (IR8a or IR25a) and two additional IRs that determine ligand binding specificity (Abuin et al., 2011; Silbering et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a model based on established knowledge, supported by citations to Abuin et al., 2011 and Silbering et al., 2011.

claim: Up to three GRNs, including many sweet and bitter GRNs, co-express IR25a and IR76b.
source: Consistent with gene expression arrays (Cameron et al., 2010), we showed in this paper that up to three GRNs, including many sweet and bitter GRNs, co-express IR25a and IR76b.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2 and citation to Cameron et al., 2010.

claim: IR25a and IR76b play central roles in sweet GRNs in a multimeric receptor complex for initiating appetitive taste behavior to fatty acids.
source: Based on these findings and with consideration of their established role in other sensory systems, we propose that IR25a and IR76b play central roles in sweet GRNs in a multimeric receptor complex for initiating appetitive taste behavior to these chemicals.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data and inference from established knowledge about IR function in other systems.

claim: Both IR25a and IR76b are co-expressed in two other GRNs of most tarsal taste sensilla, strongly arguing for additional taste functions.
source: Intriguingly, both genes are also co-expressed in ﻿﻿﻿ two other GRNs of most tarsal taste sensilla, strongly arguing for additional taste functions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the expression data showing IR25a and IR76b in multiple GRN types.

claim: The third GRN (the sour GRN) is narrowly tuned to acids in an IR25a/IR76b dependent manner.
source: While the subset of tarsal bitter GRNs activated by hexanoic acid does not require either gene, we have discovered that the third GRN (the sour GRN) is narrowly tuned to acids in an IR25a/IR76b dependent manner (Chen and Amrein, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen and Amrein, 2017.

claim: Modality specific IRs are likely expressed in a cell-type specific fashion whereby they complement IR25a/IR76b to function as either a fatty acid or a sour taste receptor.
source: These observations suggest that modality specific IRs are likely expressed in a cell-type specific fashion whereby they complement IR25a/IR76b to function as either a fatty acid or a sour taste receptor.
evidence: This is a proposed model inferred from the observation that IR25a/IR76b function in different taste modalities with different cell-type specific IR subunits.

claim: The most responsive GRN for sugars is the one associated with the 5v sensilla, followed by that with the 5s and finally the 5b sensilla.
source: First, we note the difference in sensitivity of appetitive GRNs to sugars and fatty acids, respectively: The most responsive GRN for sugars is the one associated with the 5v sensilla, followed by that with the 5s and finally the 5b sensilla, while the responsiveness for fatty acids is the reverse (5b > 5s > 5v; Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 4.

claim: The responsiveness of GRNs for fatty acids is the reverse of that for sugars (5b > 5s > 5v).
source: First, we note the difference in sensitivity of appetitive GRNs to sugars and fatty acids, respectively: The most responsive GRN for sugars is the one associated with the 5v sensilla, followed by that with the 5s and finally the 5b sensilla, while the responsiveness for fatty acids is the reverse (5b > 5s > 5v; Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 4.

claim: Fatty acids induce weaker PER responses from stimulation of the labial palps as opposed to tarsi.
source: Second, fatty acids induces weaker PER responses from stimulation of the labial palps as opposed to tarsi, while sugars induce equally strong PER responses from stimulation of either taste organ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Fujii et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by PER data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Fujii et al., 2015.

claim: Sugars induce equally strong PER responses from stimulation of either the labial palps or tarsi.
source: Second, fatty acids induces weaker PER responses from stimulation of the labial palps as opposed to tarsi, while sugars induce equally strong PER responses from stimulation of either taste organ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Fujii et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by PER data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to Fujii et al., 2015.

claim: At least some fatty acids activate bitter GRNs.
source: Third, at least some fatty acids activate bitter GRNs (Figure 6), and hence, generate more complex activation patterns in the brain than sugars, which are not known to activate neurons other than sweet GRNs.
evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ imaging data in Figure 6 showing bitter GRN activation by hexanoic acid.

claim: Sugars are not known to activate neurons other than sweet GRNs.
source: Third, at least some fatty acids activate bitter GRNs (Figure 6), and hence, generate more complex activation patterns in the brain than sugars, which are not known to activate neurons other than sweet GRNs.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Sugars but not fatty acids are soluble in water.
source: Finally, sugars but not fatty acids are soluble in water, and hence, the specific solvents in which these chemicals are presented provides different textural quality, which was recently shown to play a role in taste perception (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established chemical knowledge, with citation to Zhang et al., 2016 for the role of texture in taste perception.
